ANNEX ON PERFORMANCE BY POLICY SECTORS
The Medium-Term Expenditure Framework (MTEF) approved by the Government and the annual budget approved by the Parliament are the main documents that allocate public funds to achieve the objectives of the National Development Strategy (NDS), the Kosovo Economic Reform Program (KERP), the National Program for the Implementation of the Stabilization and Association Measures (NPISAM), and other strategic documents. Similar to other countries, Kosovo operates under conditions of limited resources, making it essential that every euro from collected public revenues is strategically allocated to activities that address the most pressing needs for the competitiveness of the economy and the well-being of the country's citizens.
To this end, the Government of Kosovo has approved the Public Financial Management Strategy with the strategic aim of improving the performance approach in the budget cycle. This is regulated by Article 21.l (paragraph l, point ii) of the Law on Public Financial Management and Responsibilities, which requires “a list of measurable objectives that are used to assess the success of a budget organization in fulfilling its mission.” This serves as information to enhance accountability and dialogue with legislators and citizens on policy issues.
Similar to the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework (MTEF) 2025-2027, this performance annex is divided into sixteen policy sectors. This approach is based on the international classification of COFOG (Classification of Government Functions) developed by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), which is used by all major international entities, such as the United Nations and the European Union, among many others.
Each sector in this annex is divided into three parts. The first part includes the objectives of the respective sector. The second part presents the objectives of the current budget cycle taken from the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework to establish a strategic link between the medium-term and annual budget perspectives. Finally, the third part of each sector presents the key measurable indicators.
At this stage, there are still no measurable values for some indicators due to the unavailability of reliable data.
1. PUBLIC ADMINISTRATION
1.1. Within this sector, the objectives are good governance, enhancing effectiveness and accountability, socio-economic development, advancing the country's integration processes, strengthening the international subjectivity of the Republic of Kosovo, and advancing and modernizing the entire public administration to serve efficiently, transparently, professionally, and impartially to all citizens, businesses, and the institutions of the Republic of Kosovo, creating conditions for the sustainable return of displaced persons, protection, integration, and development of communities living in Kosovo.

2. PUBLIC FINANCE
2.1 The main aim within this sector is the sustainability and management of public finances in accordance with the strategic framework and obligations under the European integration agenda, as well as ensuring the implementation of priorities in maintaining fiscal discipline to preserve macro-fiscal stability that guarantees sustainability and economic growth. The advancement of fiscal policies will be oriented to ensure support and fair treatment of economic entities, increase tax revenues and formal employment, as well as intensify efforts to eliminate tax evasion, combat the informal economy, and fight against money laundering. Additionally, there is a goal for greater engagement in increasing the efficiency and effectiveness of public procurement, strengthening electronic procurement, as well as increasing the transparency of public tenders, to achieve a fair ratio between value and expenditure.
2.2 The main objectives of this sector are:
Harmonization of legislation in the field of Public Finances in accordance with the  obligations arising from the Stabilization and Association Agreement (SAA) and international standards; Ensuring the implementation of fiscal discipline to maintain macro-fiscal stability;  Increasing allocative efficiency in public money management to provide quality services  to citizens; Increasing operational efficiency in public money management, in accordance with  applicable rules and standards; Ensuring sound public finances through reforms in Public Financial Management and  cooperation with International Financial Institutions; Reducing tax evasion, the informal economy, and money laundering;  Advancing the electronic procurement system, increasing efficiency and effectiveness, as  well as transparency in public tenders, ensuring equal treatment and value for money; A transparent and digitized system for managing public finances. 

MACRO-FISCAL FRAMEWORK 2024-2026
1. Global Economy
Global growth, although unsatisfactory, is expected to remain stable. Economic growth is estimated to be around 3.2% in 2024 and 2025, which is almost the same from the forecasts of July and April of this year. However, there have been revisions for various countries, from where the upward forecasts for the United States have been offset by the downward revision of forecasts for other developed economies, especially for the largest European countries. The latest forecasts for global growth show that after five years economic growth will fluctuate around 3.1%, which remains much weaker compared to the average economic growth before the pandemic. Enduring structural constraints such as population aging and lack of productivity are constraints affecting potential growth in many economies. Although this largely reflects China's weaker outlook, medium-term prospects in other regions, such as Latin America and the European Union, have also worsened.
Cyclical imbalances have softened since the start of the year, leading to a better alignment of economic activity with potential output in major economies. This alignment has made inflation rates in different countries close to each other and has generally contributed to the reduction of global inflation. Despite the tightening of monetary policy around the world, the global economy has remained remarkably resilient during the deflationary process, avoiding a global recession.

Global inflation is expected to decline from an annual average of 6.7% in 2023 to 5.8% in 2024 and 4.3% in 2025, with developed economies reaching their inflation targets faster than developing economies. Despite the fact that the global "battle" against inflation has been largely won, inflationary pressures persist in some countries and the path to price stability is still possible.
Although commodity prices have stabilized, service price inflation remains high in many regions, almost twice as high as before the pandemic. Some emerging market economies are facing a return of inflationary pressures, sometimes due to high food prices. The rise and then fall in global inflation reflects a combination of shocks: supply disruptions coupled with strong post-pandemic demand pressures, followed by sharp increases in commodity prices caused by the war in Ukraine and tensions in the Middle East. It is difficult for monetary policy to maintain price stability when faced with shocks that simultaneously increase prices and decrease output. As supply disruptions eased and monetary policy began to tighten to curb demand, the normalization of labor markets allowed inflation to fall rapidly without a major slowdown in economic activity. Major central banks in developed economies have begun to cut their interest rates, moving their monetary policy toward neutrality, helping to keep inflation expectations steady. Figure 2. Forecast for inflation rate
Volatility in the financial markets as occurred in early August may affect the tightening of financial conditions and affect investment especially in developing economies, where large external financing needs in the short term may trigger capital outflows and difficulties in return of debts. Intensification of protectionist policies would exacerbate trade tensions, reduce market efficiency and further disrupt supply chains. Rising social tensions could cause social unrest, damaging consumer and investor confidence and potentially delaying the adoption and implementation of necessary structural reforms. In many countries, there is an urgent need to shift to fiscal policies in order to ensure the stabilization of debt dynamics and to rebuild the much needed fiscal reserves, however, this should be adapted to the specific circumstances of the country. While lowering interest rates provides some fiscal relief by lowering funding costs, it will not be enough, especially when real long-term interest rates are much higher than pre-pandemic levels. 2. Recent Economic Developments in Kosovo
The year 2023 was characterized by stable economic growth of 4.1% in real terms and 8.8% in nominal terms, while inflation showed a slowing trend, reaching 4.9%. According to data from the Kosovo Agency of Statistics (KAS), the growth of economic activity continued into the first half of 2024. This growth was primarily driven by consumption, which grew by 7.2% in real terms and contributed 7.35 percentage points to the GDP growth.
Inflation—the harmonized consumer price index—rose by an average of 1.9% during the period January-September 2024, showing a significant downward trend (from an average rate of 5.8% in the same period last year). The categories with the highest increases were: the “Food and non- alcoholic beverages” category, with a rise of 1.9%, “Household supply, equipment, and routine maintenance” with an increase of 3.0%, “Housing, water, electricity, gas, and other fuels” with an increase of 4.1%, while the “Transport” category saw a decline of 0.7%, reflecting the drop in international oil prices during this period.
Total investments (private and public) in the first half of 2024 grew by 2.8% compared to the first half of 2023, contributing positively by 1 percentage point to GDP growth.
On the other hand, net exports in the first half of 2024 increased by 9.4%, with a negative contribution of 3.4 percentage points. Exports rose by 10.5% (goods exports by 4.8% and services exports by 12.8%), contributing 3.1 percentage points to economic growth (goods exports 0.4 percentage points and services exports 2.7 percentage points). Imports grew by 9.1% (6.1% for goods imports and 23.1% for services imports), with a negative contribution of 6.6 percentage points (goods 3.6 percentage points and services 2.9 percentage points).
The current account deficit during the period January-July reached -564.4 million euros, a notable increase of about 41.2% compared to the same period last year.
The trade in goods during 2024 continued to reflect the effects of rising prices. The trade deficit in goods expanded by around 8.8%. Meanwhile, the surplus in services recorded an annual increase of 3.8%.
Goods exports grew by 7.9%, while services exports recorded an annual growth of 12.9%.
According to the latest data on the structure of goods exports, there was a decline in the share of other manufactured articles in total exports (13.2% compared to 21.4% last year); a decrease in the share of the category "base metals and articles thereof" to 20.8% of total exports, and the category "plastics, rubber, and articles" with a share of 13.4%. In terms of contribution to the reduction of goods exports, the most significant impact came from the export of other manufactured articles with 9.0 percentage points, base metals and articles thereof with 6.1 percentage points, and plastics, rubber, and articles thereof with 1.4 percentage points.
Services exports grew by 12.9% compared to the same period last year. This growth was mainly driven by travel services, with a contribution of 10.7 percentage points, computer, information, and telecommunications services, and construction services, each contributing 2.5 percentage points, and other business services with a contribution of 5.4 percentage points.
Goods imports grew by 8.7% compared to last year, driven primarily by the category "transportation means" (3.1 percentage points), textiles and articles thereof (1.6 percentage points), and machinery, tools, and electrical equipment (1.1 percentage points), offset by the negative contribution of the "mineral products" category with 4.4 percentage points, and the "plastics, rubber, and articles thereof" category with a negative contribution of 1.3 percentage points. Meanwhile, services imports grew by 24.6%, mainly driven by a significant increase in the import of travel services, contributing 11.4 percentage points, transportation services by 5.7 percentage points, and other business services by 4.5 percentage points.
Figure 3. Current Account Balance
The balance of primary income during the January-July 2024 period saw a decline of 28.6% compared to the same period last year, while the balance of secondary income remained at the same levels as the same period last year.

Figure 4. Labor Market
The economic activity developments this year and last year are also reflected in the labor market. The employment data published by the Kosovo Agency of Statistics only provide information up to 2023. According to this data, the unemployment rate in 2023 averaged 10.7% (compared to 11.9% the previous year), while the labor force participation rate averaged 42.3% (compared to 38.5% in 2022).
As official data from the Kosovo Agency of Statistics for the labor market is available only up to the end of 2023, this section also includes data from the Kosovo Tax Administration, which provides administrative data on the labor market. According to this aggregated data for the first half of 2024, an average of 413,500 people were employed, representing an annual increase of about 4.1%.
Figure 5. Loans, Deposits, and Non-Performing Loans, January-August
Bank loans has continued to be a stable source of financing for the economy. At the end of August 2024, the stock of loans reached a value of around 5.4 billion euros, marking an increase of 14.9% compared to the previous year. The stock of corporate loans grew by 11.2%, while household loans grew by 20.0%.
Deposits continued to grow, primarily driven by household deposits. At the end of August 2024, the total stock of deposits reached around 6.5 billion euros, registering an annual increase of 10.6%. The stock of corporate deposits grew by 10.4%, while household deposits grew by 8.9%. In terms of deposit types, transferable deposits saw an annual increase of 8.1%, contributing 5.2 percentage points to the total deposit growth. The level of non-performing loans (NPL) reached 2.1% at the end of August 2024, marking a slight deterioration from the same period last year (2.0%). 3. Macroeconomic Perspective
According to the Ministry of Finance, Labor, and Transfers (MFPT) estimates, Kosovo’s economy is expected to grow by about 4.5% in real terms and 6.6% in nominal terms during the current year. Based on the latest data from the Kosovo Agency of Statistics, the economy has continued its growth trend.
The expectation for an average real economic growth of 4.5% in 2024 represents a downward revision by 0.2 percentage points compared to the previous round of projections made in April 2024. This is mainly due to the downward revision of the contribution from investments (positive contribution from 2.7 p.p. to 1.6p. p), mainly due to the slower execution of capital investment, exports of goods and services is revised downwards with 0.7.p.p. (from 2.6 p.p to 1.9 p.p.) also downward revision of consumption with 0.2p.p. ( from 4.6 to 4.4) and imports with 2.2p.p. (from a negative contribution of 5.6 percentage points to a negative contribution of 3.4 percentage points).
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is expected to fluctuate around the level of 2.0% during 2024, remaining significantly lower than the level recorded in 2023 (4.9%). The inflation trend has been influenced by price developments in international food, energy, and oil markets, due to the escalation of the conflict in Ukraine and geopolitical tensions.

After moderate growth this year, Kosovo's economy is expected to grow at a faster pace in the following year (2025), with an estimated growth of around 5.6% in real terms and 7.4% in nominal terms.
Unlike 2024, the main contribution to economic growth in 2025 is expected to come from private consumption, exports of services as well as investments (both private and public). Public investments are expected to have a faster execution dynamic, not only due to new projects but also due to the continuation of existing projects whose implementation is expected to accelerate. The increase in the minimum wage, the continuation of the increase in bank loans, although at a slower rate than the current year, as well as the increase in a number of social transfers (child allowances and pensions) will continue to support the growth of private consumption in the year next year, while remittances will also continue to increase, but with an accelerated trend than the current year. Meanwhile, public consumption will increase due to the increase in the salary coefficient in the public sector and the increase in spending on government goods and services.
The export of goods and services will continue to have a positive contribution, but at a higher level compared to 2024 (with differences between the contribution of goods and services). This is mainly due to the base effect, increased goods exports, and stabilization of basic goods prices in international markets.
Imports of goods and services will continue their upward trend, with key factors for this increase being the rise in capital investments and travel services.
In the following year (2025), based on expectations for commodity prices in international markets, inflation in Kosovo is expected to decrease to 1.8% and stabilize around an average of 1.6% in the medium term.
However, the baseline inflation and economic growth projections are surrounded by downside risks, related to further increases in basic commodity prices in international markets, a stronger economic slowdown in our main trading partners, or developments that may occur in Kosovo's energy sector.
4. Government Revenues and Expenditures
4.1 Revenues and Expenditures for January-September 2024
Preliminary data for the period January-September 2024 show that budget revenues and expenditures increased compared to the same period last year. More specifically, budget revenues (including GDP) reached a value of 2,264.5 million euros, marking a growth of 7.1% compared to the same period in 2023. On the other hand, budget expenditures (including GDP) reached 2,000.2 million euros, increasing by 9.5%. However, revenues achieved a higher rate of realization than expenditures compared to the projections at the beginning of the year. Considering the flow of revenues and expenditures, the overall budget balance registered a surplus of 232.0 million euros for this period.
Revenues from direct taxes increased by about 8.1% on an annual basis for the period January- September 2024, reaching a value of 390.8 million euros. This growth was also driven by an increase in the number of employees in the private sector. Among the categories of direct revenues, personal income tax revenues increased by about 9.8% compared to the previous period, while corporate income tax increased by 8.1%. It is worth noting that property tax, after the recent reassessment, recorded a decline during this period by a rate of 33.7%.
Revenues from indirect taxes have shown significant growth as they are directly linked to the increase in the value of imported goods. According to customs data, regular imports for the period January-September 2024 increased by 8.3%. Revenues from indirect taxes during this period increased by 10.8% compared to January-September 2023, reaching a value of 1,669.0 million euros. While customs duty revenues grew at an annual rate of 11.5%, annual growth in border VAT revenues was 9.5% for the period January-September 2024. Excise taxes, one of the highest contributors to indirect revenues, also recorded an upward trend, growing by a rate of 12.6% during the reporting period.
Non-tax revenues during this period reached a value of 256.5 million euros, marking a growth of 30.0% on an annual basis. The highest growth among non-tax revenue categories was recorded by central level revenues, with an increase of 38.6%, followed by concession taxes at around 26.3%; this was due to the rising trend in the number of passengers at Pristina International Airport.
Regarding budget expenditures, all categories contributed positively to their increase for the period January-September 2024. The category of wages and allowances recorded an annual growth of 13.0%. Expenditures on goods and services also increased by 9.6%, reaching 281.8 million euros. Subsidies and transfers saw a slight increase of 1.1%, with no significant movements compared to the same period in 2023.
Capital expenditures during the period January-September 2024 recorded a significant increase of 23.1% compared to the same period in 2023. The structure of capital expenditure financing for the period January-September 2024 is dominated by the regular budget with around 77.1%, followed by dedicated revenues (8.8%), own revenues (6.8%), external borrowing financed by the investment clause (4.2%), and regular external borrowing (3.2%).
Interest expenditures during the period January-September reached a value of 32.3 million euros, recording an annual decrease of 1.7%.
4.2. Revenue Forecast for 2025 and the Medium Term
Budget revenues for the medium term are expected to grow by around 8.0% during the medium- term period, mainly as a result of continued measures undertaken by the Government, voluntary compliance, and the formalization of the economy.
Indirect tax revenues will continue to have the highest share in total revenues, at around 73.6% in 2025, and are expected to grow by about 8.1% compared to the 2024 Budget.
Direct tax revenues in 2025 are expected to increase by about 9.7% compared to the 2023 Budget, accounting for 17.7% of total revenues.
Figure 7: Structure of Budget Revenues
Non-tax revenues in 2025 are projected to increase by 21.7% compared to the 2024 budget law, reaching a total of around 356.6 million euros.
Grants for 2025 are expected to reach a value of 22.5 million euros, which represents a decrease compared to the previous year. This decline compared to last year is due to the one-time EU grant received in 2024, valued at 7.5 million euros, to support the energy sector.
In the period 2026-2027, total budget revenues are expected to grow by an average of 7.4%. Direct taxes are expected to have an average growth of 7.7% in the period 2026-2027; indirect taxes are expected to grow at an average rate of 8.6%, and non-tax revenues are expected to follow their historical trend with an average growth of 1.0%.
4.3 Expenditure Forecast for 2025 and the Medium Term
Total budget expenditures in 2025 are expected to grow by 8.8% annually compared to the 2024 Budget. The largest impact on the increase in budget expenditures comes from the measures implemented by the Government to enhance the well-being of citizens.
Total current expenditures in 2025 are planned to grow by 9.1% compared to the 2024 Budget, reaching a value of 2,614.7 million euros.

Expenditures for the category of wages and allowances are planned to be 916.9 million euros, marking an increase of 13.8%. This increase is due to the rise in the wage coefficient. Expenditures in the category of goods and services are planned to grow by 3.5% compared to the 2024 Budget. Subsidies and transfers in 2025 are expected to increase by 8.9%, mainly due to increased transfers for pensions and child allowances. Meanwhile, 4.1 million euros have been allocated for the category of current reserves.
Capital expenditures are expected to increase by 8.4% in 2025, making up 25.8% of total expenditures. During this period, the implementation of capital projects is expected, based on a priority list that includes projects impacting the improvement of the transportation network, energy network, and improvements in education, social, and healthcare systems. Most capital investments are expected to be funded by the regular budget, although many projects in various sectors are planned to be financed through external borrowing via the investment clause.
Figure 8: Structure of Budget Expenditures
In the following years, 2026-2027, total expenditures are planned to grow by an average of 5.8%. Current expenditures in 2026-2027 are planned to increase by an average of 5.3%. Capital expenditures are planned to grow at an average rate of 7.1% (9.1% in 2026 and 5.0% in 2027).
4.3.1 Central Level Expenditures 2025-2027
The budget planned for the central level for 2025 is projected to increase by 9.7% compared to the planned expenditures in the 2024 Budget for the central level. The largest increase is planned in the category of salaries and allowances, at 21.7%, as a result of increased coefficients and filling vacant positions. Additionally, the category of subsidies and transfers is expected to rise by 8.7%. On the other hand, expenditures for goods and services are planned to remain at the same level. Capital expenditures are expected to increase by 9.4% compared to the budget for 2024.

Informative Space 1. Comparison of Projections for 2025 in the 2024 and 2025 Budget Laws
Based on the projections for 2025, the main changes between the projections of fiscal and macroeconomic indicators presented in the Budget Law for 2024 and the Budget Law for 2025 have been identified. Compared to the Budget Law for 2024, the current projections for 2025 have partially changed due to the factors listed below: Upward revision of budget revenues by approximately €111.8 million:
 Base effect - Better revenue performance in 2024 compared to the projections in the 2024 Budget Law has influenced a higher revenue projection for 2025.  Direct revenues are expected to increase due to the rise in the number of employed individuals, the effect of the increase in the minimum wage, the formalization in the labor market, and the growth in business turnover.  The increase in revenues from indirect taxes will result from the rise in revenues from excise duties and Value Added Tax. The increase in the imports of capital goods will also impact the growth of revenues from indirect taxes.
Upward revision of budget expenditures by approximately €105.3 million:
 Increase in the public sector wage bill by €87.7 million as a result of filling vacant positions.  Decrease in the projected capital expenditures by € 8.6 million, as a result of better planning by Budget Organizations. Additionally, the revision of the list of potential borrowing has influenced the increase in capital expenditures financed by investment clauses. Table 4. 5. Budget Deficit and Fiscal Rules
The overall budget deficit for 2025 is expected to be €300.3 million, or about 2.7% of GDP, while the deficit according to the fiscal rule is anticipated to fluctuate around 2.0% of GDP.
In the following years (2026 and 2027), the budget deficit is projected to be 2.8% of GDP in 2026 and 1.7% of GDP in 2027, while the deficit under the fiscal rule is expected to remain the same at 2.0% in 2026 and 1.7% in 2027. Meanwhile, the usable bank balance is expected to be at sufficient levels, around 2.3% of GDP in 2025; approximately 2.6% and 3.0% of GDP in 2026 and 2027, respectively.
6.Financing and State Borrowing
Throughout the period 2025-2027, the need for financing will primarily be covered by external and internal borrowing. The Government of Kosovo has several sources of financing: (a) borrowing from the domestic market through Securities, (b) obtaining loans from international financial institutions; (c). In 2025, no revenues from liquidation funds are anticipated. During 2025, the bank balance is estimated to be around 2.5% of the projected GDP for that year. However, depending on the forecast and updating of budget revenue collections and expenditure execution throughout the budget year, the Minister of Finance, Labor, and Transfers may decide on a lower issuance of domestic debt compared to the projected amount of domestic debt in Table 1 of this law.
In the medium term, total debt, including government guarantees, is expected to reach 21.1% in 2025, 23.0% in 2026, and 24.0% in 2027.

FISCAL RISK STATEMENT
Overview Fiscal risk is the exposure of public finances to unforeseen or uncertain events that can lead to fiscal outcomes deviating from expectations presented as the ‘central case’ budget forecast (e.g deviations from the medium-term projections presented in the Law on Budget Allocation for the year 2025). The sources of fiscal risks are diverse and can arise from multiple factors. These factors include unexpected developments in the global or domestic economy, changing conditions in financial or commodity markets, through to natural disasters or public health emergencies. Longer- term fiscal risks and spending pressures are clearly emerging from climate change and can also arise from changes in the population and age-profile of the labour force. Managing fiscal risks requires a better understanding of the nature, likelihood and impact of such factors. The management of fiscal risk and its integration with fiscal planning and budget preparation has found increasingly widespread application worldwide.
This Fiscal Risk Statement provides a summary of potential risks and uncertainties that the economy of Kosovo may face, and in the event of materialization, would impact the baseline expectations of fiscal indicators within the medium term. As the Covid-19 pandemic showed, the materialization of fiscal risks can be extremely costly for an economy. Therefore, identifying, analyzing, reporting and managing fiscal risks is necessary for every government.
This statement will be updated on a regular basis and published as an annex of the Law on Bugetary Allocation, the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework, and/or the Economic Reform Programme. It is important to note that while the annex to the Law on Budgetary Allocation will generally undergo minor updates, the primary and substantial updates will be reflected in the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework. The publication of this document is an important element in the process of strengthening economic governance and constitutes one of the structural benchmarks expected to be fulfilled within one of the instruments of the Program with the International Monetary Fund, approved on 25 May 20231.
The Statement contains separate analysis of macroeconomic risks (mainly originating from the external environment), recent fiscal peformance and a range of other specific fiscal risks. Consistent with previous versions, the statement includes analysis of the performance of public- owned enterprises and now also includes an analysis of Kosovo’s debt, on-lending and guarantees, a section on public private partnerships and an overview on the robustness of the financial sector. This document provides a qualitative discussion of the main risks and, where possible, a quantitative analysis and outlines the measures or actions to prevent or moderate the impact of each risk. The drafting and publication of this Statement is intended to increase fiscal transparency and assist policy makers to better understand the nature and magnitude of fiscal risks in order to
1 https://www.imf.org/en/News/Articles/2023/05/25/pr23180-kosovo-imf-exec-board-sdr-80m-sba-sdr-61m-res-sfa put in place the appropriate policies to prevent or mitigate the consequences in case of their materialization.
Fiscal risks The fiscal risks included in this Statement are classified as high, medium or low risk, using the IMF analytical tool (FRAT: Fiscal Risk Assessment Tool)2, based on two criteria: the impact of fiscal risk and the likelihood of the risk materializing. The assessment is designed to be dynamic hence, future verisons of this statement may include additional risks depending on the circumstances and the likelihood and impact of some risks may also evolve over time depending on the economic environment and other factors.

Macro-Fiscal risks 2.1.1 Macroeconomic Risks The macroeconomic outlook for any country is naturally uncertain, and forecasts, which guide fiscal planning, rely on data, models, and expert judgment about the most likely future trajectory for the economy. Although these forecasts, underpinning the MTEF and budget, include a balance of judgments, actual outcomes rarely match expectations precisely. Models and judgments may be reasonable at the time but imperfect in hindsight, and unanticipated events and external shocks can drive deviations from the forecast. This section outlines the macro-fiscal risks and projections for 2025, emphasizing how factors, such as geopolitical tensions and inflation may impact Kosovo’s economic and fiscal outlook.
The macro-fiscal projection for 2025 show that GDP for 2025 will reach 5.6% in real terms. Increases in children allowances and pensions, and the increase in wages in private sector due to increase in minimum wage, will be the main drivers of increase in private consumption. On the other hand, the main drivers for the increase in public consumption will be the increase in the wage coefficient for the public sector and higher spending for goods and services due to municipal elections. The increase in investments is attributed to a faster execution of capital spending in outgoing projects, an increase in FDI as well as a rise in investments loans. Net exports will continue to remain in the negative territory, despite the increase in the export of goods.
Budget revenues are projected to increase by 9.2% compared with the Budget Law for 2024. The main contribution in increase is from indirect taxes by 5.9 p.p. with increase of 8.0% compared to Budget Law 2024. Non tax revenue is expected to have a 2.1 p.p contribution (21.7% increase), while direct direct taxes is set to give a 1.7 p.p contribution (9.7% increase). Budget expenditures are projected to increase by 8.8%, in comparison to the previous year. Current expenditure is estimated to increase by 9.0% (6.5 p.p. contribution) and capital expenditure is predicted to rise by 8.3% (2.1 p.p. contribution). The overall budget deficit is projected to be 2.7% of GDP, while the deficit according to fiscal rule is set at 2.0% of GDP. Bank balance is projected to reach 3.4% of GDP.
The baseline macroeconomic and fiscal scenario that underpins the medium-term projections results from a careful consideration of both downside and upside risk factors associated with economic developments expected over the medium term, incorporating judgment around a number of these identified risks. Systematic downside risk factors, which originate from long standing structural constraints that define Kosovo’s growth model (e.g., low export competitiveness, reliance on high inflow of remittances, high trade deficit) continue to be important downside risk factors.
The risks surrounding the baseline scenario during 2025 generally arise from external factors and their potential impact and likelihood continues to be elevated. In this regard, vigilance is crucial due to the many linkages of our economy with the global economy, especially through two channels: trade and remittances. Domestically, ongoing challenges in the energy sector, fiscal risks from public enterprises and risks from contingent liabilities arising from on-lending are some of the specific risks that are reflected in this document, whereas upward pressures on prices due to climate change and geopolitical tensions are some of the external risks. Over the medium-term, the potential impact of macro-fiscal risks remains the same as in the previous year, but with a greater probability of occurrence.
The baseline scenario of the macro-fiscal projections presented in the Law on Budget Appropriations in 2025 is subject to numerous downside risks, primarily originating from the external environment and beyond the government's control.
Geopolitical tensions - The possibility of further intensification of the war in Ukraine and Middle East may bring new disruptions to the supply chain, which can affect global trade and energy markets, in particular, and may drive unexpected increases in the prices of food, energy and oil. The impact of the conflict in the Middle East on oil prices has been modest so far, but an escalation could have powerful impacts on financial conditions, energy prices, global output and inflation more generally.
Remittances - is the other channel through which these international developments can affect economic activity in our country, from diaspora mainly living in major European countries. A potential surge in prices there would erode the real incomes of Kosovar emmigrants, and in our country, it would be reflected in a decrease in remittances, a decrease in travel services, and/or a decrease in foreign direct investments. A decrease in these inflows would reduce private disposable incomes (and thereby lower consumption) and private-sector investment, which would lead to lower GDP and consequently lower budget revenues than those projected. In addition, a tightening of financial conditions would continue to negatively affect financing costs, bank lending and, consequently, the demand for goods and services in the economy of Kosovo.
Monetary policy in other countries – considering the numerous interconnections of our economy with those abroad, there is a need for increased caution in the transmission of monetary policy tightening among Kosovo’s major trading partners. An increase in interest rates could potentially lead to higher costs for goods imported to Kosovo, leading to higher imported inflation.
Climate change - is another factor which can affect domestic inflation, which can cause a decrease in the production of cereals in different states, causing an increase in food prices. The reduction of electricity production from fossil fuels in order to protect the environment and the insufficient compensation for renewable energy sources can present shortages in production and thus increase energy prices which can drive broader price increases.
The table below provides an estimate of the sensitivity analysis of GDP projections for the years 2025, 2026 and 2027, showing how changes in inflation and capital expenditures (CAPEX) affect real GDP compared to the baseline scenario.

As can be seen in a scenario where inflation increases by 0.5 percentage points (p.p.), GDP growth is expected to slow down to 4.9% in 2025, 5.8% in 2026, and 6.1% in 2027, indicating a negative impact of higher inflation on economic growth. On the other hand, under-execution of capital expenditures by 10 p.p, has a softer impact on real GDP growth values. Overall, both higher inflation and under-execution of CAPEX lead to slower GDP growth, with inflation having a more pronounced effect.
2.1.2 Budget performance Preliminary data for January-September 2024 indicate that revenue realizations are generally consistent with our projections for this period (Table 3). The largest variance in budget revenues was observed in non-tax revenues. However, other revenue categories are largely in line with projections, with only minor deviations.
In contrast, expenditures were lower than the budgeted amounts for the same period. Expenditures during this period were under-executed, particularly capital expenditures. However, in line with usual realization patterns, a higher rate of capital expenditures is expected for the last quarter of the year. On the other hand, historically, current expenditures have consistently exceeded projections, however for the above-mentioned period they reached a realization of 91.0%.
As a result, the bank balance for the period Jan-Sep of 2024 is EUR 232.0 million.

Specific Risks 2.2.1. Fiscal Risks from Debt, On-lending and Guarantees
The Law on State Debt and State Guarantees includes several provisions that ensure fiscal stability: the total debt ceiling including state guarantees may not be higher than forty percent (40%) of GDP, as well as certain limitations on municipal borrowing.
The state debt at the end of 2023 was 1,663 million Euro, of which 970 million Euro is domestic and 693 million Euro is external debt (Table 4). The public debt to GDP ratio has maintained a relatively steady downward trajectory in recent year, falling from 22.4% in 2020 to 17.5% in 2023. In 2020, the debt-to-GDP ratio saw a significant rise due to the additional funding required to combat the economic crisis triggered by COVID-19. However, thanks to strong budget revenue performance from the economic recovery in 2021 and stronger than expected nominal GDP growth in 2022, among other factors, the government was able to build fiscal buffers and reduce the need for new debt issuance, resulting in a steadily declining debt-to-GDP ratio to pre-pandemic levels.

As of the latest update for January-June 2024, the debt-to-GDP ratio stands at 15.8%, with a total debt stock of EUR 1,662 mln. So far, the composition of debt remains relatively stable, with 42% of external debt and 58% of domestic debt. For the existing portfolio, the average time to maturity is 6.3 years while the weighted average interest rate is 2.6%. Government guarantees, which represent contigent liabilities, have decreased to EUR 4.08 mln, reflecting strategic efforts to minimize fiscal risks by scaling back on guarantees.
Guarantees and On-lending
In Kosovo's state debt structure, a potential source of risk is loans guaranteed by the public sector and international on-lending for companies that supply key services to the public. The debt portfolio at the end of 2023 included two state guarantees (Urban Traffic Prishtinë and a second guarantee for the Credit Line of the Kosovo Deposit Insurance Fund) worth EUR 29 million. There is no municipal debt or municipal guarantees issued. A previous guarantee for the Kosovo Deposit Insurance Fund expired at the end of December 2023. On the other hand, on-lending to companies that supply key services to the public reached 18.8 million Euro.
The segments that require a more detailed observation are state guarantees for Urban Traffic and sub-loans to enterprises that provide public services. A weak performance by these enterprises could impose a dual burden on the government: it might need to subsidize the services provided and manage the financial responsibilities assumed towards external creditors. However, given the low value of outstanding guarantees and sub-loans, the impact is currently assessed as low. This coupled with the expiration of the Kosovo Deposit Insurance Fund guarantee represents a positive shift in reducing overall fiscal risk.
Actions to mitigate contingent liabilities from on-lending and state guarantees
To minimize the risks posed by on-lending and guarantees, measures such as monitoring the financial condition of beneficiaries and regularly assessing the likelihood of realization of these liabilities will continue to be implemented. Based on the estimates of the expected losses, guarantee fees will be set according to the criteria of the Law on Public Debt, the secondary legislation for which is being drafted. Additionally, the oustanding value of guarantees is included within the calculation of general debt, hence ongoing compliance with the the debt to GDP ratio limit would help managing these risks. Furthermore, an additional measure that has been taken in order to manage these risks is the inclusion of a position in the Law on Budget Allocation as a budget allocation for losses from guarantees in case of failure in their repayment by the main borrower.
2.2.2. Fiscal Risks from Public Enterprises
Overview of the Public Enterprises Sector
Publicly Owned Enterprises (POEs) can exert a significant influence on fiscal outcomes, particularly when unexpected subsidies, loans, or capital injections (equity) become necessary, contingent liabilities are realized, or tax and dividend revenues fall short of projections. Furthermore, POEs indirectly affect fiscal indicators through their impact on economic growth. The likelihood of fiscal risks emerging from publicly owned companies increases when POEs are undercapitalized, operate at a loss, or face liquidity constraints.
In Kosovo, Public-Owned Enterprises (POEs) are categorized in two groups: central and local government-owned. The central level includes 19 enterprises, 17 overseen by the Ministry of Economy, one (KOSTT) by the Assembly, and one (Gjakova Airport) by the Kosovo Security Force (KSF). For the case of Trepça, its ownership is split, with the state holding 80% and workers 20%. A new central public-owned enterprise, the Energy Storage Corporation (ESC), has been established to manage 125 megawatts of battery storage capacity being developed through the Compact Program with the U.S. Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC). This enterprise will be included in future analyses of fiscal risks from central-level POEs. The following analysis is based on financial data from 17 central government public enterprises, operating in the energy, transport, water supply, telecommunications and mining sector, supervised by the Ministry of Economy. Figure 2 below gives a representation of POEs by sector, it is evident that the majority of these enterprises are part of the water supply sector.
Figure 2 - Number of POEs by sector
The graphs below (Figure 3) present a more detailed overview of the audited financial statements for the public enterprise (POE) sector over the period 2019 to 2023. The reports show that the total assets of the 17 public enterprises increased from €1.408 billion in 2019 to €1.686 billion in 2023. Total revenues have grown since 2019, with a significant increase in 2022, largely driven by fluctuations in energy prices. This increase had a direct impact on net profit. In 2023, the POE sector recorded a profit of €2.3 million, with more than half of the enterprises operating at a profit. Overall liabilities remain manageable, despite their increase over this period, due to the strong liquidity position of the largest public enterprises, which exert the most significant influence across the all sectors.

The return on equity for 2023 was notably low at 0.2 percent, representing a significant decrease from the 11.1 percent return on equity recorded in 2022. Despite improvements in operational performance among public enterprises compared to the previous year, this decline occurred due to KOSTT's substantial net loss, which adversely impacted the overall net profits of the public enterprise sector.
As can be seen in Figure 4 below, the outstanding debt held by POEs is relatively concentrated among the largest entities. Overall, publicly-owned enterprises continued to generate profits in 2023, leading to an improvement in their liquidity positions. As a result, these enterprises are now better equipped to meet their financial obligations.
Figure 4 - Liabilities by POEs (in '000) and their cumulative participation to total liabilities of the POE sector (in %)
To provide a comprehensive overview of the profitability, liquidity, and solvency of the portfolio of public enterprises, the audited financial statements for 2023 have been analysed using six key financial indicators: the cost coverage ratio, return on equity, the current ratio, debtor turnover days, debt-to-asset ratio, and debt-to-EBITDA ratio (Figure 5). These indicators have been carefully calculated, and each has been assigned a risk rating in accordance with internationally recognized financial standards, ensuring consistency and comparability. The risk ratings of public enterprises range from Category 1 – the lowest risk – to Category 5 – the highest risk.

Over the years there were notable trends in both improvement and deteriorations. Initially, in 2019 and 2020, there were no companies classified under "Very Low" or "Low" risk, indicating a higher overall risk profile during these years.
Figure 5 - Distribution of companies across various risk levels (2019-2022)
However, in 2021, 6% of companies moved into the "Low" risk category, and by 2022, this figure doubled to 12%, signalling some improvements in risk management. Meanwhile, the "Moderate" risk category showed stability in 2019 and 2020 (41%) but dropped to 24% in 2021 before rising slightly to 29% in 2022. The most significant trend is seen in the "High" risk category, which surged from 47% in 2019 to 65% in 2021, before improving to 41% in 2022, reflecting effective measures to manage high-risk companies. Despite this, the "Very High" risk category, which decreased from 12% in 2019 to 6% in 2020 and 2021, spiked to 18% in 2022. This indicates that while overall risk levels improved, a small but significant portion of companies became more vulnerable, requiring focused risk management efforts.
In 2023, as seen from Figure 6 below, 6% of companies are considered to be low risk (Category 2), 29% moderate risk (Category 3), 53% are categorized as high risk (Category 4) a slight increase from the previous year, and 12% fall into the very high-risk category (Category 5), signalling a continuation of efforts to manage high-risk companies.

2.2.3. Public Private Partnerships
Kosovo’s Public-Private Partnership (PPP) portfolio remains relatively modest but it still demonstrates a significant contribution to the country’s infrastructure development.
Currently, Kosovo has three fully operational PPPs:
1. Adem Jashari Internationa Airport – has an investment value of EUR 100 milion and started operating since 2013. Planned to enhance the airport’s infrastructure and operational capacity, this PPP included plans for the construction of a new terminal, a modern navigation tower, and an expanded partking lot.
2. High School Complex in Gjilan – has an investment value of EUR 800,000, started in 2013 and has a 15-year lifespan.
3. Underground Parking in Prishtina – has an investment value of EUR 12 million, started construction in 2020 and has a lifespan of 35 years.
The total investment value for these operational PPP projects amounts to EUR 112.8 million.
Additionally, the municipality of Prishtina is advancing an important project currently under in the construction phase which involves the development of three new schools representing an investment of EUR 16.6 million with a 10-year lifespan. In the tendering phase, the Municipality of Podujeva proposed construction of an underground parking facility valued at EUR 2.9 million and is designed to be in this partnership for the next 30 years. Looking ahead, the 75 MW Wind Energy Plant is in the feasibility study stage, with an estimated investment of approximately EUR 113 million.
These projects collectively are expected to contribute to the country's infrastructure, education and sustainable energy development.
2.2.4. Financial Sector
The financial sector plays a cruicial role, by facilitating credit and insurance services that support economic activity. Considering its key impact, any distruption in the financial system can trigger implications in the economy. Therefore, as it is done regularly, it is necessary to be supervised by the Central Bank of Kosovo (CBK) in order to mitigate risks or intervene when needed.
The Central Bank of Kosovo publishes an annual Financial Stability Report (FSR), providing a detailed assessment of the financial sector’s risks and performance. The latest report, published in 2023, reviewed the sector's performance in 2022, highlighting key risks driven by global and regional macroeconomic conditions.
For 2022, CBK identified increased uncertainty and risks stemming from external factors, including the war in Ukraine, which affected global commodity prices, economic growth perceptions, and tightened financing conditions. Locally, while Kosovo's fiscal position improved due to rising prices, this was accompanied by negative effects on the current account deficit as import prices surged. That being said, the report indicates that despite these challenges, Kosovo's financial system remained stable, but with heightened vulnerabilities linked to global economic dynamics and local fiscal pressures.
It’s notable that over the past decade, the financial system in Kosovo has not needed to extend budgetary assistance in the last ten years, such as bailouts or capital infusions into any of the institutions comprising it. Kosovo’s financial sector remained sound and well-functioning even in the face of extreme challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic, in part due to policy measures that supported the economy, businesses and households through that period.
Given the low historical need for government intervention, fiscal risks in the financial sector are considered minimal. However, continued CBK monitoring is crucial to maintaining stability, even when conditions appear healthy.
In 2023, Kosovo's financial sector continued to demonstrate resilience despite ongoing global and regional challenges. While risks remained elevated due to external factors, such as the war in Ukraine and the resulting global economic volatility, Kosovo's financial institutions maintained sound operations. To present such overview of 2023, Table 5 compiles financial indicators, drawing on data from the CBK’s Monthly Financial System Reports for the year.
As exhibited in Table 5, Kosovo’s financial sector in 2023 was predominantly led by commercial banks, which held the largest share of total assets and demonstrated strong profitability and return on equity (ROE). Microfinance institutions, despite being smaller in scale, also performed well, marked by high market concentration and healthy profitability indicators. Insurance companies, while less concentrated and with fewer assets, maintained stable profitability. Across all three abovementioned sectors, foreign ownership was significant, especially in commercial banks and microfinance institutions. Solid loan quality and overall sector stability was reflected by non- performing loans as well which remained low for all institutions. Additionally, pension funds displayed consistent asset levels and steady growth throughout the year.

Based on the Monthly Financial System Reports from the Central Bank of Kosovo for January to August 2024 we note that the financial sector is currently displaying stable overall profitability and growth.

Similarly, profitability displays an upward positive trend of growth, indicating that financial conditions in this sector are stable. Concluding Remarks
Quantifying fiscal risks is a complex process with intensive data requirements, therefore at this early stage, the analysis has selected and addressed only some of the identified risks. Drafting this Statement demands extensive collaboration across various parties within and beyond the Ministry, alongside the utilization of sophisticated analytical tools.
It is worth noting that MFLT has quickly adapted to the demand for increased attention to fiscal risks by creating a special division for their analysis and monitoring in the last year. As the quantity and quality of data increases, as well as the advancement of internal capacities to implement the analytical tools required to address these risks, this Statement will be further expanded to provide an ever more accurate picture of fiscal risks.
